summary:
We developed NEPTUNI II, a web-based health monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It combines clinical records, health tracking over time, a 3D body map for locating symptoms, standardized psychological well-being questionnaires, and a radiation monitoring module.

The radiation module combines manually entered personal dosimeter readings with simulated environmental telemetry to show cumulative exposure and how it changes over time. An experimental remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) module uses a camera to estimate pulse rate and pulse rate variability (PRV) while assessing signal quality.

NEPTUNI II organizes each astronaut’s records into a timeline, compares readings with baseline values, and shows trends throughout the mission. Reminders help crew members keep track of pending check-ins, and alerts highlight changes that may warrant medical evaluation.

On long missions, communication with Earth can be delayed. Keeping health records organized and accessible on board can help crews track their health and share findings with the medical team.

The demo uses sample data and simulations. Its results are for demonstration purposes only and do not constitute clinical measurements or medical diagnoses.
details:
What exactly does it do?

NEPTUNI II is a web prototype that helps astronauts monitor their health during long-duration missions. It lets crew members:

  • Record symptoms, locate discomfort on an interactive 3D body map, and answer follow-up questions about the affected area.
  • Complete standardized well-being questionnaires and review earlier assessments.
  • Log personal dosimeter readings, record symptoms after an event, and explore simulated radiation scenarios for the International Space Station, the Moon, and Mars.
  • Estimate pulse rate with a standard webcam using experimental remote photoplethysmography (rPPG).
  • Schedule check-ins around the length of the mission and review Medicine, Well-being, and Radiation records in one timeline.

How does it work?

  1. Set up the mission. The crew member opens a demo session with an alias, enters the mission duration, and chooses how often to complete a medical check-in. The plan can also schedule a well-being check every 14 days when the mission is long enough.
  2. Record symptoms and check in. In Medicine, the crew member selects a body region or symptom and answers follow-up questions. When a response triggers an alert, the interface explains which reported finding prompted it. In Well-being, the crew member can complete WHO-5, PHQ-9, or GAD-7, with PHQ-4 available as a brief additional check. Saving the required assessments updates the reminder.
  3. Track radiation-related records. The crew member enters personal dosimeter readings manually and can link a post-event follow-up to a recorded event. The simulator generates labeled synthetic telemetry inspired by the Canadian Space Agency’s CANS instrument. The experiments section includes a comparison of published Radi-N2 measurements and an EVARM-inspired form for logging readings before and after a spacewalk.
  4. Estimate pulse rate with a camera. The rPPG module tracks facial regions and applies the Plane-Orthogonal-to-Skin (POS) method to estimate pulse rate from changes in reflected light. The local demo also runs a model trained on UBFC-rPPG data to assess signal quality. Camera frames are processed on the device.
  5. Review and share the record. The My Space Health view shows entries in UTC, identifies their source, and links back to the original records. The crew member can export a summary for review and resume the demo later with the same alias in the same browser.

What benefits does it have?

  • For the crew, check-ins and reminders make it easier to follow up on symptoms and keep track of what is due during a busy mission.
  • For the medical team, a timeline and shareable summary provide a clearer account of what changed, when it was reported, and what measurements or events were recorded around that time.
  • For mission simulations, teams can practice documenting a health event, reviewing an alert, and preparing a handoff under simulated communication delays.

What do we hope to achieve?

In the short term, we want to test the full workflow in simulated missions and observe how easily users can complete a check-in, find a previous record, and explain why an alert appeared. In the longer term, we want to work with clinical and mission specialists to validate the workflows and define the procedures and data protections needed for operational use.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Web interface and 3D map. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js.
  • Camera module. React, TypeScript, Vite, and MediaPipe Face Landmarker.
  • Machine learning. Python and scikit-learn’s ExtraTrees classifier for training, with ONNX Runtime Web for browser inference.
  • Hardware. A standard computer and webcam for the local demonstration.
  • Data and references. UBFC-rPPG for model training, published Radi-N2 measurements for the historical comparison, NASA resources for spaceflight health and medical operations, and Canadian Space Agency resources for CANS and EVARM.

How did we use artificial intelligence?

  • Machine learning in the rPPG module. We trained an experimental ExtraTrees classifier using the UBFC-rPPG dataset and exported it to ONNX. In the local demonstration, the classifier assesses the quality of the webcam signal. The POS signal-processing method estimates pulse rate.
  • OpenAI Codex for software development. We used Codex to assist with code implementation, debugging, and testing as we integrated the rPPG module and developed the radiation workflows and mission reminders.
  • ChatGPT for research and writing. We used ChatGPT to help organize research notes, summarize technical documents provided by the team, and draft and translate the project submission.

What makes the project creative, and what did we consider?

The project connects tools that would otherwise be used at different points in a health check. A crew member can pinpoint discomfort on a 3D map, document how it changes, and review it alongside a dosimeter reading or mission event in the same timeline. We designed the reminders around crew workload and rest periods, using an optional display window and a snooze action. The demo labels simulated readings, preserves the source of each record, and uses the timeline to show the order of events. Clinical interpretation and operational decisions remain with qualified personnel.
